F1.quote: Academ-AI documents examples of suspected undeclared AI usage in the academic literature, discernible primarily due to the appearance in research papers of idiosyncratic verbiage characteristic of large language model (LLM)-based chatbots.
F1.claim: what it is: a documentation of suspected undeclared AI use in the literature, discernible mainly by chatbot verbiage

F2.quote: The consensus of the academic publishing community is that such usage must be declared in the published article.
F2.claim: the publishing community's consensus: AI use in writing must be declared in the article

F3.quote: This analysis of the first 768 examples collected reveals that the problem is widespread, penetrating the journals, conference proceedings, and textbooks of highly respected publishers.
F3.claim: the paper analyses the first 768 examples: the problem is widespread, in journals, proceedings and textbooks of highly respected publishers
F3.lineage: the dataset paper: the first 768 cases

F4.quote: Undeclared AI seems to appear in journals with higher citation metrics and higher article processing charges (APCs), precisely those outlets that should theoretically have the resources and expertise to avoid such oversights.
F4.claim: undeclared AI seems to appear in journals with higher citation metrics and higher APCs
F4.lineage: where it appears: higher APCs and citation metrics

F5.quote: An extremely small minority of cases are corrected post publication, and the corrections are often insufficient to rectify the problem.
F5.claim: an extremely small minority of cases are corrected, often insufficiently
F5.lineage: after publication: corrections, formal and stealth

F6.quote: The 768 examples analyzed here likely represent a small fraction of the undeclared AI present in the academic literature, much of which may be undetectable.
F6.claim: the governing limit: the 768 are likely a small fraction; much undeclared AI may be undetectable
F6.lineage: the selection's limit: the detectable trace

F7.quote: Publishers must enforce their policies against undeclared AI usage in cases that are detectable; this is the best defense currently available to the academic publishing community against the proliferation of undisclosed AI.
F7.claim: publishers must enforce their policies where use is detectable, the best defence available

F8.quote: [Submitted on 20 Nov 2024 ( v1 ), last revised 15 Nov 2025 (this version, v2)]
F8.claim: the paper: v1 20 November 2024, v2 15 November 2025
F8.lineage: the dataset paper: its versions and venue

F9.quote: In: Arai, K., Lorenz, P. (eds) Intelligent Systems and Applications. IntelliSys 2026. Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems, vol 2077. Springer, Cham
F9.claim: the paper's journal reference: IntelliSys 2026, Springer LNNS vol. 2077
F9.lineage: the dataset paper: its versions and venue

F13.quote: Phrases characteristic of AI-generated text were used to query Google Scholar.
F13.claim: cases are found by querying Google Scholar with phrases characteristic of AI text

F14.claim: each result is examined by hand against inclusion and exclusion criteria

F15.claim: the paper excludes any medium other than journal articles, conference papers and books

F16.claim: the paper's dataset: 768 documents, 633 journal articles, 107 conference papers, 28 book chapters

F17.quote: 44% of the documents in the Academ-AI dataset make a similar reference to their training cutoff.
F17.claim: 44% of the documents refer to a training cutoff

F20.quote: approximately one in four of these evaded detection by a major publisher with an explicit policy against such content.

F21.quote: the journals committing editorial oversights concerning AI are paradoxically paid more for editorial processing and achieve greater academic impact.

F21.lineage: where it appears: higher APCs and citation metrics

F22.quote: The examples on Academ-AI were predominantly identifiable due to characteristic turns of phrase, which are only reproduced in a manuscript when authors copy text directly from an AI system with little to no scrutiny.
